guide.summary: Unit 6 compares energy sources: how fossil fuels, nuclear power, biomass, solar, hydroelectric, geothermal, hydrogen, and wind produce usable energy, where they are found, and their environmental trade-offs. Energy calculations (kWh, cost, efficiency, fuel required, half-life) are among the most frequently tested skills on the exam.

sections.heading: Energy use and fossil fuels
sections.body: Nonrenewable sources (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium) form or exist in finite amounts; renewable sources (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass if harvested sustainably) are replenished on human timescales. Developed nations use far more energy per capita; global use is dominated by fossil fuels. Coal forms from ancient plant matter buried in swamps under heat and pressure (peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite, increasing carbon content and energy). Oil and natural gas form from marine organisms. In a power plant, fuel's chemical energy becomes heat, which boils water to steam that turns a turbine connected to a generator; typical efficiency is about 30–40%, with the rest lost as heat. Natural gas emits roughly half the CO₂ of coal per unit of electricity, but methane leaks offset some of that benefit. Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) unlocks gas in shale but can contaminate groundwater, uses large volumes of water, and wastewater injection can trigger earthquakes. Tar sands and oil spills cause habitat destruction.

sections.heading: Nuclear and biomass
sections.body: Nuclear fission of U-235 releases heat to make steam; it emits no CO₂ during operation but produces radioactive waste with long half-lives, thermal pollution, and risk of accidents (meltdowns). Mining uranium also disturbs land. After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ of a radioactive sample remains. Biomass (wood, crop waste, ethanol, biodiesel) can be renewable but releases particulates and CO₂; corn ethanol is not carbon-neutral because fossil fuels are used to grow and process it, and it competes with food crops and drives land-use change.

sections.heading: Renewables and storage
sections.body: Solar photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly to electricity; active and passive solar heating capture heat. Solar is intermittent and needs storage or backup, and panels require mining of metals. Hydroelectric dams provide steady, controllable power but block fish migration, trap sediment, flood habitat, and can release methane from decaying flooded vegetation. Geothermal uses Earth's internal heat and is most practical near plate boundaries and hot spots. Hydrogen fuel cells combine H₂ and O₂ to produce electricity with water as the only exhaust, but most hydrogen is currently made from natural gas and is costly to store. Wind turbines produce no emissions during operation; power increases with the cube of wind speed, so siting matters; drawbacks include intermittency, bird and bat mortality, and visual impact.

sections.heading: Conservation and calculations
sections.body: Conservation includes LED lighting, efficient appliances, insulation, passive solar design, public transit, carpooling, and higher fuel-efficiency standards. Key units: power in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW); energy = power × time, in kilowatt-hours (kWh). Cost = kWh × price per kWh. Efficiency = useful output ÷ input. To find fuel required: energy needed ÷ efficiency ÷ energy content per unit of fuel. Always carry units through each step.

sections.heading: Worked example: energy calculations
sections.body: A 100 W light bulb runs 5 hours per day for 30 days: 100 W × 150 h = 15,000 Wh = 15 kWh. At $0.15 per kWh, the cost is $2.25. Replacing it with a 15 W LED uses 2.25 kWh, costing about $0.34, a savings of about $1.91 per month. AP Environmental Science free-response questions often require multistep calculations like this; show units at every step and use scientific notation for large values.

sections.heading: Comparing energy sources
sections.body: Coal is abundant and cheap but releases the most CO₂, sulfur dioxide, and particulates per unit energy. Natural gas burns cleaner but leaks methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and extraction by fracking raises concerns about groundwater contamination. Nuclear power has low carbon emissions but produces long-lived radioactive waste and carries accident risk. Renewables such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric produce little pollution during operation but are intermittent or site-dependent, requiring storage or grid management.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students forget to convert watts to kilowatts, confuse energy (kWh) with power (kW), and list advantages without disadvantages.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know nonrenewable and renewable energy, fossil fuels, fracking, nuclear fission, half-life, biomass, photovoltaic cells, wind turbines, hydroelectric dams, geothermal energy, hydrogen fuel cells, and energy conservation.

keyTakeaways: Fossil fuel plants: chemical → thermal → mechanical → electrical; ~30–40% efficient.
Natural gas emits less CO₂ than coal, but methane leaks matter.
Nuclear: no operational CO₂; long-lived waste.
Dams: steady power but block fish and trap sediment.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by efficiency when calculating fuel input.
Saying hydrogen fuel cells emit CO₂ at the tailpipe.
examTips: FRQ calculations need every step with units; dimensional analysis earns points.
Know one specific advantage and disadvantage for every energy source.
Watch for questions about where a resource is located (geothermal near plate boundaries, hydro needs elevation drop).
For half-life problems, count the number of half-lives first.
guide.cramSheet:
**Fossil:** coal (plants) · oil/gas (marine) · plant: fuel → heat → steam → turbine → generator

**Gas vs coal:** ~½ CO₂ · fracking: water, quakes, methane

**Nuclear:** fission U-235 · no CO₂ · waste, thermal pollution · (½)ⁿ

**Biomass:** not always carbon-neutral · particulates

**Solar:** intermittent · **Hydro:** fish, sediment · **Geo:** plate boundaries · **H₂:** water exhaust · **Wind:** P ∝ v³

**Math:** kWh = kW × h · cost = kWh × $ · input = output ÷ efficiency

vocab.definition: A resource that exists in a finite amount or forms far more slowly than it is used.

Splitting a heavy nucleus (U-235) into smaller nuclei, releasing energy.
Time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.
A device that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
Building design that captures and stores solar heat without mechanical systems.
A device that combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity and water.
Energy used by a 1 kW device running for one hour.
Ratio of useful energy output to total energy input.
An energy source that is not continuously available, such as solar or wind.

distractors.A: Uses 4 as the denominator instead of 2⁴.

practice.stem: Which is an environmental disadvantage of a large hydroelectric dam?

choices.text: It emits large amounts of sulfur dioxide during operation.
It cannot adjust output to meet demand.
It blocks fish migration and traps sediment that would otherwise replenish downstream habitats.

practice.explanation: Dams fragment rivers and starve downstream deltas and floodplains of sediment.

distractors.B: Dams can adjust output quickly; that is an advantage.

choices.text: the injection of large volumes of wastewater into deep disposal wells

practice.explanation: High-pressure wastewater injection can lubricate and stress existing faults.

practice.stem: Which is the most significant challenge to using solar photovoltaic panels as a city's only source of electricity?

choices.text: Output varies with time of day and weather, so energy storage or backup is required.

practice.explanation: Solar is intermittent; demand continues at night and on cloudy days.

practice.stem: Which statement best explains why corn-based ethanol is not fully carbon-neutral?

choices.text: Fossil fuels are used to make fertilizer, run farm machinery, and distill the ethanol.
Burning ethanol releases more CO₂ than the corn absorbed while growing.

practice.explanation: Even if combustion CO₂ equals what the crop absorbed, the production chain adds fossil emissions.

practice.frqType: Q3 Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution Doing Calculations
practice.prompt: A family uses 900 kWh of electricity per month, all from a grid powered mostly by coal and natural gas. They are considering a 5.0 kW rooftop solar photovoltaic system. Their location averages the equivalent of 5.0 hours of full sun per day. The system costs $15,000, and a 30% tax credit reduces that cost. Electricity costs $0.15 per kWh, and the grid emits an average of 0.40 kg of CO₂ per kWh. Assume 30 days per month.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the electricity, in kWh, the system will produce per month. Show your work.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the family's annual savings on electricity bills, assuming all solar electricity replaces grid electricity. Show your work.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the payback period, in years, after the tax credit. Show your work.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of CO₂ the system prevents each year. Show your work.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Describe one environmental disadvantage of producing or disposing of solar panels.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Propose one energy conservation measure the family could adopt and explain how it reduces electricity use.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Identify one renewable energy source that could supply the family at night, and explain why.

rubric.description: E.g., mining metals (silicon, silver, rare metals) disturbs habitat; manufacturing uses energy; panels contain toxic materials (e.g., cadmium, lead) that can leach from landfills.
E.g., LED lighting, Energy Star appliances, added insulation, programmable thermostat, line-drying clothes.
Explains how the measure delivers the same service with less electricity (e.g., LEDs convert more electricity to light and less to heat).
E.g., wind (blows at night), geothermal or hydroelectric from the grid (continuous), or battery storage charged by solar (must explain availability).

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) 5.0 kW × 5.0 h/day × 30 days = 750 kWh per month.

(b) 750 kWh/month × 12 months = 9,000 kWh/yr × $0.15/kWh = $1,350 per year.

(c) Net cost = $15,000 × (1 − 0.30) = $10,500. Payback = $10,500 ÷ $1,350/yr ≈ 7.8 years.

(d) 9,000 kWh/yr × 0.40 kg CO₂/kWh = 3,600 kg CO₂ avoided per year.

(e) Manufacturing panels requires mining metals such as silver and silicon, which disturbs habitat and generates mine waste.

(f) Replace incandescent bulbs with LEDs. LEDs convert a much larger share of electricity into light instead of heat, so they use about one-sixth the electricity for the same brightness.

(g) Wind energy, because wind often blows at night, when solar panels produce nothing.
